newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Nobel peace laureate attacks Australian PM.
newsitem.headline: Nobel peace laureate attacks Australian PM.

text.p: Nobel peace prize winner Jose Ramos Horta said on Thursday that Australian Prime Minister John Howard's approach to Aborigines was based on a "bankrupt argument" and "meanness".

In contrast, Horta praised former Labor prime minister Paul Keating as a statesman who showed leadership in 1993 when he apologised for crimes committed against Aborigines, the most disadvantaged group in Australian society.

Horta, citing Germany's apology for the Holocaust, said he could not understand why Howard would not issue a government apology to Aborigines forcibly taken as children from their parents under government assimilation policies.
"Sometimes we must recognise that atrocities begin at home," Horta said in a speech on human rights at the University of New South Wales.

"To say that an apology promotes a 'black armband' view of history is a bankrupt argument. Such an argument itself promotes... a 'white blindfold' view of history," said Horta, the East Timorese independence leader and joint winner of the 1996 Nobel peace prize.
"Apologising is a show of maturity, self-confidence and generosity. They are the attributes that elevate a country in the eyes of the world."

Australia's human rights commission in May issued a report on the "Stolen Generation", the tens of thousands of Aborigines taken from their parents, labelling the assimilation practices from the 1880s to the 1960s as attempted genocide.
The report also called on the national government to apologise and to compensate Aborigines.

Howard has issued a personal apology to the "Stolen Generation" but has refused to apologise on behalf of the government, arguing that modern Australia should not feel guilty about the past. He says to feel guilty about the past is a "black armband" view of Australian history.
There are an estimated 300,000 Aborigines in Australia's 18 million population. Aborigines have a life expectancy 15 to 20 years less than the rest of Australia's population.
Horta also criticised Howard's moves to extinguish Aboriginal native title rights on farm land.
"To seek to deny the native title rights of Aborigines, who have after all gained them fairly and through the due process of law, white man's law, is meanness," Horta said.
In 1976, Aborigines in the outback Northern Territory gained the first and only inalienable land rights in Australia.
But in 1993 the Keating government passed native title laws covering all of Australia after a court ruled that Aborigines had ownership of land prior to European settlement in 1788.

Native title was thought to cover only unused government land. In 1996, however, the High Court of Australia ruled native title could co-exist with farmers' rights, sparking warnings from farmers that their livelihoods were at risk.
Howard, under pressure from farmers who dominate his junior coalition government partner, the National party, is moving to extinguish native title on pastoral land.
Horta also criticised Australia for its stance on East Timor, arguing it had lost Australia a United Nations Security Council seat last October.
Australia, one of a handful of Western nations to recognise Indonesian sovereignty over East Timor, was defeated by Portugal for the U.N. Security Council seat.
"For the new Australian government, it was a humiliating defeat at the hands of a small European country usually derided by foreign affairs bureaucrats in Canberra," Horta said.
"Portugal's dignified stance on the issue of East Timor played a part in its victory."
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 after Portugal abandoned the colony in 1974 and annexed the territory in 1976. The United Nations does not recognise Indonesian sovereignty over East Timor.
